- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). content.text: I have everything I need — all structural claims are empirically verified. Delivering the design.

input.approach_name: Layered `tsl` + `cxx` split with `#[path]`-included modules under a package-root bin (three layers: generic hopscotch core → map facade → C++ runtime shims → thin entry)
module_layout: /output/Cargo.toml -> Package manifest ONLY. `edition = "2021"`, empty `[dependencies]`, `[profile.release] opt-level = 3`, and a single explicit target: `[[bin]] name = "test15", path = "test15.rs"`. Deliberately NO `[lib]` section, NO `src/lib.rs`, NO `src/main.rs` — cargo's target auto-discovery then contributes nothing, so the package-root `test15.rs` is the one and only crate root under both build commands.

/output/test15.rs -> The crate root for BOTH `cargo build --release` and `rustc test15.rs`. Contains exactly three things and no logic: (1) the crate-level doc comment, (2) the module wiring `#[path = "src/tsl/mod.rs"] mod tsl;` and `#[path = "src/cxx/mod.rs"] mod cxx;` and `#[path = "src/app.rs"] mod app;`, (3) a ~15-line `fn main()`. VERIFIED: `#[path]` on a module declared in the crate root resolves relative to the directory containing the crate-root FILE, not the process cwd — I compiled the same tree as `rustc test15.rs` from the package dir AND as `rustc /tmp/dbe/test15.rs` from `/tmp`, and both linked all five module files and produced identical output. This is what makes the dual-build requirement work verbatim.

/output/src/tsl/mod.rs -> Facade for the `tsl` namespace. Nothing but `pub mod hash; pub mod hopscotch_hash; pub mod hopscotch_map;`, the `pub use` re-exports that let callers write `tsl::HopscotchMap`, a module doc comment mapping each C++ name to its Rust counterpart, and `#![allow(dead_code, unused_imports)]` for the whole layer. NOTE: because this file is reached via `#[path = ".../mod.rs"]`, it acts as a directory owner, so its children are plain `mod` declarations resolving to siblings in `src/tsl/` — the `#[path]` attribute is needed only twice, in the crate root. Verified.

/output/src/tsl/hash.rs -> The `std::hash` substitute layer; knows nothing about tables. `IdentityHasher` + `BuildIdentityHasher` reproduce libstdc++ `std::hash<integral>`, which is `static_cast<size_t>` of the value (so `write_i32` should sign-extend: `self.state = i as i64 as u64`, matching `(size_t)(-1) == 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF`; under power-of-two low-bit masking this is indistinguishable from `i as u32 as u64`, but sign extension is the faithful transcription). `write` falls back to FNV-1a so `&str`/`[u8]` keys still spread. `MixingHasher` + `BuildMixingHasher` provide a murmur3 `fmix64` full-avalanche finalizer for hostile key distributions. Both are `BuildHasher` impls, so the table is pluggable.

/output/src/tsl/hopscotch_hash.rs -> The generic hopscotch core, `HopscotchHash<K, V, S = BuildIdentityHasher>` where `K: Hash + Eq, S: BuildHasher`. Owns the bucket array, the neighbourhood bitmaps, the overflow vector, the load factor, growth/rehash, and all `Pos` arithmetic. Every public method is expressed in terms of `Pos` (a plain index newtype) — no lifetimes and no iterator types appear at this layer, which is what keeps the borrow checker out of the algorithmic code. It has no notion of 'map' vs 'set' semantics beyond storing a `(K, V)` tuple per slot.

/output/src/tsl/hopscotch_map.rs -> The `tsl::hopscotch_map` layer: a newtype wrapping `HopscotchHash` that adds (a) the C++-shaped surface the ported test names — `insert((k, v))` taking ONE tuple to mirror `map.insert({i, i * 12})`, `equal_range`, `count`, `find`, `begin`, `end` — and (b) the safe borrow-checked iterator types `Iter`, `EqualRange`, `Keys`, `Values` that convert a raw `Pos` into `(&K, &V)` yields. This is the only `tsl` module the entry file talks to.

/output/src/cxx/mod.rs -> Facade for the C++ runtime-compat layer: `pub mod stoi; pub mod argv; pub mod terminate;` plus re-exports. Physically separate from `src/tsl/` because it is a different kind of thing — emulation of libstdc++/libc behavior rather than a container — and because it must stay dependency-free of `tsl` (the dependency arrows run entry -> {tsl, cxx, app}, app -> tsl, cxx -> nothing; no cycles).

/output/src/cxx/stoi.rs -> A pure `std::stoi` clone over BYTES: `pub fn stoi(s: &[u8]) -> Result<i32, StoiError>` and `pub enum StoiError { InvalidArgument, OutOfRange }`, plus a private `fn is_c_space(b: u8) -> bool` matching the exact C-locale set `{0x20, 0x09, 0x0A, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0D}`. Zero I/O, zero process control, no panics — which is precisely why the ~90 vectors in the behavioral spec can all become `#[test]` cases in this file. Also the natural home for `pub fn stoi_pos(s: &[u8]) -> Result<(i32, usize), StoiError>` (the two-arg C++ overload) even though the program never calls it.

/output/src/cxx/argv.rs -> argv plumbing and the program's option gate. `pub struct Argv(Vec<Vec<u8>>)` captured via `std::env::args_os()` + `OsStrExt::as_bytes()` (NEVER `env::args()`, which panics on non-UTF-8 where the C++ binary happily returns 5 for bytes `0x35 0xFF`), with `from_env()`, `argc()`, `get(i) -> Option<&[u8]>`. `pub fn resolve_count(argv: &Argv) -> Result<i32, Fault>` encodes the gate `argc > 1 && argv[1] == b"--a"` and returns `Ok(15)` when the gate fails, `Err(Fault::NullString)` when `argv[1] == b"--a"` but `argv[2]` is absent, and `Err(Fault::Stoi(e))` otherwise. `pub enum Fault { NullString, Stoi(StoiError) }`.

/output/src/cxx/terminate.rs -> libstdc++ `std::terminate` emulation, the single place any byte of stderr is produced. `pub fn terminate_with(exception: &str, what: &str) -> !` writes `format!("terminate called after throwing an instance of '{exception}'\n  what():  {what}\n")` (two-space indent, TWO spaces after the colon) then calls `std::process::abort()`. Three named wrappers hide the strings: `logic_error_null_string()`, `stoi_invalid_argument()`, `stoi_out_of_range()`. VERIFIED byte-identical: my Rust `eprint!` + `abort()` produced a stderr file that `cmp`'d equal to the C++ binary's 87-byte stderr, both dying `Aborted (core dumped)` with shell status 134.

/output/src/app.rs -> The ported program as a PURE function, so the observable output is unit-testable in-process without spawning a binary: `pub fn build_map(count: i32) -> HopscotchMap<i32, i32>` and `pub fn num_in_range(count: i32) -> usize`. `main` then reduces to: `let argv = Argv::from_env(); let count = match resolve_count(&argv) { Ok(c) => c, Err(f) => f.terminate() }; println!("{}", app::num_in_range(count));`. `build_map` deliberately does NOT pre-reserve capacity, so the rehash path is exercised exactly as the C++ exercises it (this is what the spec's 4095/4096/4097 and 65535/65536/65537 probes are designed to catch).

TESTS: keep every `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` INLINE in the module it covers. VERIFIED that `cargo test` compiles the bin target with `--test` and collects tests from every `#[path]`-included module (my 5-file replica reported `running 4 tests` with names `tsl::hash::tests::id`, `tsl::hopscotch_hash::tests::p`, `tsl::tests::smoke`, `compat::stoi::tests::junk`). Corollary and trap: a `/output/tests/` integration directory would NOT work, because with no `[lib]` target there is no `test15` crate to `use`; such a file would have to repeat the `#[path]` includes itself.
input.core_data_structures:
LAYER 1 — the bucket (`hopscotch_hash.rs`):

```rust
pub const NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE: usize = 32;   // bitmap is a u32
pub const INITIAL_BUCKET_COUNT: usize = 16;
pub const DEFAULT_MAX_LOAD_FACTOR: f32 = 0.9;

pub struct Bucket<K, V> {
    neighbourhood: u32,          // bit d set <=> slot (home + d) holds an entry whose home is this bucket
    entry: Option<(K, V)>,       // None == vacant slot
}
```
Two fields, not three: the bitmap is meaningful only for a *home* bucket, the `Option` only for a *storage* slot, and one bucket plays both roles independently. For `K = V = i32`, `Option<(i32, i32)>` is 12 bytes and the struct is 16 bytes — exactly four buckets per cache line, so a 32-slot neighbourhood scan touches at most 8 lines and in practice 1-2 because the bitmap tells you which slots to visit.

LAYER 1 — the table:

```rust
pub struct HopscotchHash<K, V, S = BuildIdentityHasher> {
    buckets: Vec<Bucket<K, V>>,  // len == bucket_count + NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1
    overflow: Vec<(K, V)>,       // unbounded fallback; keeps insert total
    len: usize,                  // live entries, buckets + overflow
    mask: usize,                 // bucket_count - 1; bucket_count is always a power of two
    hash_builder: S,
    max_load_factor: f32,
}
```
Three invariants carry the whole design: (1) `bucket_count` is a power of two so the modulo is `hash & mask`; (2) the vector is over-allocated by `NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1` trailing slots so a neighbourhood starting at the last home bucket never wraps — no modular index arithmetic anywhere, and those tail slots are legal storage but never home buckets; (3) `buckets[h].neighbourhood` bit `d` is set iff `buckets[h + d].entry.is_some()` and that entry's home is `h`, which is what makes lookup touch only set bits.

POSITIONS — the C++ iterator substitute:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
pub struct Pos(usize);
```
One flat, totally-ordered index space over both containers: `0 .. slots()` indexes `buckets` (where `slots() == buckets.len()`), `slots() .. slots() + overflow.len()` indexes `overflow`, and `end_pos() == Pos(slots() + overflow.len())` is one past the last. Because `Pos` is `Copy + PartialEq`, the ported loop's `first != second` and `++it` map onto `!=` and `pos_after` with no unsafe code and no lifetime entanglement — this is the single decision that keeps the core algorithms readable.

LAYER 2 — the map facade and its iterators (`hopscotch_map.rs`):

```rust
pub struct HopscotchMap<K, V, S = BuildIdentityHasher> { table: HopscotchHash<K, V, S> }

pub struct Iter<'a, K, V, S>       { map: &'a HopscotchMap<K, V, S>, cur: Pos, stop: Pos }
pub struct EqualRange<'a, K, V, S> { inner: Iter<'a, K, V, S> }   // same shape, distinct type for intent
```
An iterator is just a borrow plus two `Pos` values, i.e. a literal C++ iterator pair. `Iterator::Item = (&'a K, &'a V)`; `next()` returns `None` when `cur == stop`, else reads the entry at `cur` and advances via `table.pos_after`. `Keys`/`Values` are `Iter` + `map`.

LAYER 3 — the compat types (`cxx/`):

```rust
pub enum StoiError { InvalidArgument, OutOfRange }   // two variants: two different stderr texts
pub enum Fault { NullString, Stoi(StoiError) }       // three observable death modes total
pub struct Argv(Vec<Vec<u8>>);                       // owned bytes, not OsString, not String
```
`Fault` exists because the missing-`argv[2]` death is a `std::logic_error` with a completely different `what()` and must not be folded into `StoiError`.
algorithms: HOME BUCKET. `fn bucket_for(&self, key: &K) -> usize { let mut h = self.hash_builder.build_hasher(); key.hash(&mut h); (h.finish() as usize) & self.mask }`. Power-of-two masking only — no modulo, no prime table. VERIFIED that `Hash for i32` dispatches to `Hasher::write_i32` (not `write`), so `IdentityHasher` really does see the raw integer: hashing `5i32` yielded 5, `0i32` yielded 0, `-1i32` yielded 0xffffffff, while `"ab"` routed through `write`. That dispatch is the whole reason identity hashing reproduces the C++ performance profile.

LOOKUP — `find(&self, key: &K) -> Option<Pos>`. Compute `home = bucket_for(key)`, take `bits = buckets[home].neighbourhood`, then iterate ONLY the set bits: `while bits != 0 { let d = bits.trailing_zeros() as usize; let slot = home + d; if buckets[slot].entry.as_ref().map_or(false, |(k, _)| k == key) { return Some(Pos(slot)); } bits &= bits - 1; }`. The `bits &= bits - 1` idiom clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per occupied neighbour, never 32 times. If the bitmap is exhausted, linearly scan `overflow` and return `Pos(slots() + i)` on a hit, else `None`. Worst case is bounded by `NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE` plus the overflow length, and the overflow list is empty for every non-adversarial hasher/key combination.

INSERT — `insert(&mut self, key: K, value: V) -> (Pos, bool)`. (1) `if let Some(p) = self.find(&key) { return (p, false); }` — C++ `insert` on a duplicate key is a NO-OP that keeps the OLD value and returns `{existing, false}`; this is the property that pins `equal_range` to at most one element, so it must not be written as an overwrite. (2) Grow if `(self.len + 1) as f64 > self.bucket_count() as f64 * self.max_load_factor as f64`. (3) `let p = self.place(key, value); self.len += 1; (p, true)`. Keep `place` free of any growth check, because `rehash` reuses it.

PLACEMENT WITH HOP-BACK — `fn place(&mut self, key: K, value: V) -> Pos`, the heart of the algorithm. (a) `home = bucket_for(&key)`. (b) Linear-probe for the first vacant slot at or after home: `let mut free = home; while free < self.buckets.len() && self.buckets[free].entry.is_some() { free += 1; }`; if the probe runs off the padded end, push to `overflow` and return. (c) While `free - home >= NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE`, pull the free slot backwards: scan candidates `cand` ASCENDING over `free + 1 - NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE .. free` (ascending picks the earliest mover, which is the largest single jump); let `ch = bucket_for(candidate's key)`; the candidate may be relocated into `free` iff `ch + NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE > free` (i.e. `free` lies inside the candidate's OWN neighbourhood) and `ch <= cand`. To move it: `let e = buckets[cand].entry.take().unwrap(); buckets[free].entry = Some(e); buckets[ch].neighbourhood &= !(1u32 << (cand - ch)); buckets[ch].neighbourhood |= 1u32 << (free - ch); free = cand;` and restart the while-condition. If a full scan finds no movable candidate, the cluster is unbreakable: push `(key, value)` to `overflow` and return — this is what makes insertion total and guarantees termination even for a hasher that maps every key to one bucket. (d) Otherwise `buckets[free].entry = Some((key, value)); buckets[home].neighbourhood |= 1u32 << (free - home);`. The shift amount is provably `< 32` here because the while-loop exited, so no shift-overflow panic is possible.

GROWTH / REHASH — `rehash(&mut self, min_entries: usize)`. Compute `new_bc = max(INITIAL_BUCKET_COUNT, ceil(min_entries / max_load_factor).next_power_of_two())`, and for the automatic growth path additionally `new_bc = max(new_bc, bucket_count * 2)`. Build a fresh `Vec` of `new_bc + NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1` default buckets, `std::mem::replace` it in, `std::mem::take` the old overflow, set `mask = new_bc - 1`, then re-`place` every old entry — buckets first, then the old overflow entries. Do NOT route re-insertion through `insert`: that would re-check the load factor (re-entrant growth) and double-count `len`, which stays untouched by a rehash. Document that every previously handed-out `Pos` is invalidated, exactly as C++ iterators are invalidated by a rehash.

ITERATION ORDER — `first_pos`, `pos_after`, `end_pos`. `pos_after(Pos(i))`: if `i` is a bucket index, scan `i + 1 .. slots()` for the next `entry.is_some()` and return it; if none is found, return `Pos(slots())` when `overflow` is non-empty, else `end_pos()`; if `i` already indexes overflow, return `Pos(i + 1)` (which naturally equals `end_pos()` past the last). `first_pos()` is the first occupied bucket, else the start of overflow, else `end_pos()`. This yields a single well-defined forward order over both containers, which is the only thing `equal_range`'s second iterator needs in order to be meaningful. Do NOT attempt to reproduce the C++ iteration order — the spec establishes that only the DISTANCE (1 present / 0 absent) is invariant, not which element `range.second` names.

EQUAL_RANGE — `match self.find(key) { None => (self.end_pos(), self.end_pos()), Some(p) => (p, self.pos_after(p)) }` at the core layer, wrapped at the map layer into `EqualRange { cur, stop }`. Present => `cur != stop` once, then `pos_after` lands exactly on `stop` => exactly one yield. Absent => `cur == stop == end` => zero yields. The entry file should keep the C++ loop shape (`let (first, second) = ...; let mut it = first; while it != second { n += 1; it = pos_after(it); }`) or its idiomatic equivalent `map.equal_range(&key).count()` — but must NOT be short-circuited to `contains_key`, because then the ported test would no longer exercise the iterator machinery it exists to test. A `debug_assert_eq!(range.count(), map.count(&key))` inside the map layer's tests cross-checks the two independent paths.

STOI — `fn stoi(s: &[u8]) -> Result<i32, StoiError>`, a `strtol` transcription, NOT `str::parse`. (1) Advance while `is_c_space(s[i])` where the set is EXACTLY `{0x20, 0x09, 0x0A, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0D}` — hand-rolled, because `u8::is_ascii_whitespace` omits vertical tab 0x0B and `"\x0b1"` must return 1. (2) Consume AT MOST ONE `b'+'` or `b'-'`, with no whitespace skip afterwards (`"- 1"`, `"--1"`, `"+-1"` must all fail). (3) Require `s[i].is_ascii_digit()`; if not, `Err(InvalidArgument)`. (4) Accumulate in i64 with saturation over the maximal digit run: `acc = acc.saturating_mul(10).saturating_add((b - b'0') as i64)` — base is hard-coded 10, no `0x` sniffing, no octal, no locale grouping. (5) Stop at the first non-digit and DISCARD the entire remainder with no error. (6) Apply the sign in the WIDE type: `let v = if neg { -acc } else { acc };`. (7) Range-check `v < i32::MIN as i64 || v > i32::MAX as i64 => Err(OutOfRange)`, which yields the asymmetric accepted range that lets `"-2147483648"` succeed while `"2147483648"` fails. (8) `Ok(v as i32)`. Saturation (not wrapping) is what makes 5000 nines report OutOfRange instead of landing on a plausible small value.

ARGV GATE — `fn resolve_count(argv: &Argv) -> Result<i32, Fault>`. `if argv.argc() > 1 && argv.get(1) == Some(b"--a".as_ref()) { match argv.get(2) { None => Err(Fault::NullString), Some(b) => stoi(b).map_err(Fault::Stoi) } } else { Ok(15) }`. Exact byte comparison, no trimming and no case folding (`"--a "` and `"--A"` must fall through to 15); the `&&` short-circuit means `argv[1]` is only touched when it exists; anything past `argv[2]` is never read. VERIFIED that `args_os()` + `OsStrExt::as_bytes()` compiles and behaves identically under editions 2015 and 2021.

TERMINATION — `fn terminate_with(exception: &str, what: &str) -> !` does `eprint!("terminate called after throwing an instance of '{}'\n  what():  {}\n", exception, what)` then `std::process::abort()`. `Fault::terminate(self) -> !` dispatches: `NullString => ("std::logic_error", "basic_string::_S_construct null not valid")`, `Stoi(InvalidArgument) => ("std::invalid_argument", "stoi")`, `Stoi(OutOfRange) => ("std::out_of_range", "stoi")`. stdout must stay completely empty on these paths, so resolve the count BEFORE printing anything. `abort()` and not `process::exit(134)`: verified that `abort()` reproduces the real SIGABRT (`Aborted (core dumped)`, status 134) that an uncaught C++ exception produces, and that the resulting stderr `cmp`'s byte-identical to the C++ binary's.

PROGRAM BODY — `app::num_in_range(count: i32) -> usize`: `let mut map = HopscotchMap::new(); for i in 0..count { map.insert((i, i.wrapping_mul(12))); } let key = count / 2; map.equal_range(&key).count()`. `0..count` is empty for `count <= 0`, which reproduces the empty map and the printed `0` with no special-casing and no panic; never convert `count` to an unsigned type (`i32::MIN as usize` would be catastrophic). `wrapping_mul(12)` is mandatory, not stylistic — VERIFIED that plain `rustc` without `-O` turns overflow checks ON (a constant-folded `200000000i32 * 12` was rejected at compile time as a hard error, and a runtime one would panic with exit 101 where the C++ silently wraps). `count / 2` needs no helper: both languages truncate toward zero.

input.perf_notes:
All numbers below are from a working prototype of THIS design (same bucket layout, same hop-back loop, same overflow fallback) that I built and ran in a scratch dir, so the perf claims are measured rather than asserted. Reference: the C++ binary does 10M inserts in ~0.40 s.

Release (`-O`, 10M sequential inserts of keys 0..n-1, then `equal_range(n/2)`):
- IdentityHasher: 316 ms, final bucket_count 16,777,216, overflow 0 entries. Beats the C++ by ~20%.
- MixingHasher (fmix64): 1.37 s.
- `std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher` (SipHash-1-3): 1.75 s.

That 4-5x spread is the central performance argument for the layering, and it is NOT about hash-function cost — it is about locality. With identity hashing, key `i` has home bucket `i & mask`, so building the map from 0..n-1 walks the bucket array strictly linearly: every insert hits a cache line already warmed by its predecessor, every probe finds its home slot vacant on the first try, and no hop-back ever executes. Any mixing hasher scatters those same keys uniformly over a 268 MB array and turns a linear scan into 10M random misses. This is exactly why libstdc++'s `std::hash<int>` is the identity function and why `tsl::hopscotch_map<int,int>` is fast on this workload — so `BuildIdentityHasher` must be the DEFAULT type parameter, and `DefaultHasher` must not be (it is 5.5x slower on the very workload the acceptance test measures, and its per-process random seed would make iteration order nondeterministic between runs, which is a fidelity regression even though this program's output cannot observe it).

Choice of mixing function, measured. The angle asks whether FNV-1a or a Fibonacci mix is a better fit; for a table that masks the LOW bits of the hash, Fibonacci multiplication is actively broken, and I verified it. On an adversarial key set (5000 distinct keys all congruent to 0 mod 2^20, i.e. differing only in high bits): identity hashing put 4064 of 4096 entries in the overflow list (3.18 ms, and the linear overflow scan is what makes it quadratic as it grows); `key.wrapping_mul(0x9e3779b97f4a7c15)` then masking low bits was IDENTICALLY bad — 4064 overflow entries, 3.16 ms — because the low bits of `k * odd` depend only on the low bits of `k`, so the multiply accomplishes nothing you can see through a low-bit mask; the fmix64 avalanche finalizer dropped overflow to 0 and the time to 273 µs, a 12x win. Conclusion for the design: Fibonacci hashing is only correct paired with HIGH-bit extraction (`(k * PHI) >> (64 - log2(bucket_count))`), which conflicts with the mask-based bucket_for; since we mask low bits, the mixing hasher must be a full avalanche (fmix64), and FNV-1a should be kept only for the byte-oriented `write` path where there is no integer to mix.

Scaling and the debug path. Insert cost is linear and flat: 52 µs at 1e3, 37 ms at 1e6, 316 ms at 1e7 (~32 ns/insert). Unoptimized (`rustc test15.rs` with no `-O`, which is how the standalone build will be exercised) costs ~5x: 190 ms at 1e6 and 1.63 s at 1e7 — slower, but still linear and nowhere near pathological, and `cargo build --release` with `opt-level = 3` is the path that meets the C++ number. Memory is the real ceiling, not time: 16.8M buckets x 16 bytes = 268 MB at count=1e7, and the same 0.9 load factor as the C++, so the port will hit allocation failure at roughly the same counts the C++ does.

Micro-details that earn their keep: `bits &= bits - 1` iterates only occupied neighbours instead of all 32; `trailing_zeros` is a single instruction; `mask` is stored rather than `bucket_count` so the hot path has no subtraction; the `NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1` tail padding removes every wraparound branch from probing; `Option<(K, V)>` keeps vacancy testing to one discriminant load; and `build_map` deliberately does not pre-reserve, so the O(n) amortized rehash chain (16 -> 32 -> ... -> 16.8M, each entry re-placed via the same `place`) is exercised exactly as the C++ exercises it — the doubling makes the total re-placement work strictly less than the final pass.
risks: EDITION SKEW IS THE REAL DUAL-BUILD TRAP, not the module wiring. `cargo build` uses edition 2021 (from Cargo.toml) but `rustc test15.rs` uses rustc's DEFAULT, which is edition 2015 — the manifest is not consulted. So the source must live in the intersection of both editions. VERIFIED failures under 2015: `u8::try_from(..)` is E0599 because `TryFrom`/`TryInto` are in the 2021 prelude only (fix: an explicit `use std::convert::TryFrom;`, which is valid in both); and `[1u8,2,3].into_iter()` silently yields `&u8` under 2015 vs `u8` under 2021 (my probe failed with E0606 'casting &u8 as u32 is invalid' — but a variant that type-checks either way would compile to DIFFERENT BEHAVIOUR, which is the nastier outcome; fix: always write `.iter()` or `IntoIterator::into_iter(arr)` explicitly). Also avoid `try` as an identifier (a keyword from 2018 on), and rely on nothing from 2021 closure disjoint-capture. Mitigation: keep a CI-style checklist that BOTH `cargo build --release` and a bare `rustc test15.rs` are run before declaring done — I verified the full 5-file tree compiles clean under `--edition 2015`, `--edition 2021`, and cargo.

A `[lib]` + `use test15::tsl::...` arrangement would satisfy `cargo build` and BREAK `rustc test15.rs` (no extern crate to resolve, E0432/E0463, unless the grader passes `--extern`, which the stated command does not). The `#[path]`-include arrangement is the only one that satisfies both commands verbatim, and the cost is that the modules are compiled as part of the bin crate — so there is no library crate for a `/output/tests/` integration directory to `use`. Keep all tests inline in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` (verified that `cargo test` collects them from every `#[path]`-included module); if someone later adds `tests/foo.rs`, it will not compile without repeating the `#[path]` includes.

Identity hashing is fast on the tested workload and pathological on adversarial ones, and DOUBLING THE TABLE DOES NOT FIX IT. For keys that differ only above the mask width, every rehash reproduces the same collision set, so the entries land in the overflow list; because `find` scans that list linearly, insertion degrades to O(n^2) — measured 120 ms for a 200k-insert clustered run versus 273 µs with the avalanche hasher. The ported program's keys are 0..count-1 so it never triggers, but the LIBRARY is generic and a future caller can. Mitigations to document loudly in `hash.rs`: `BuildIdentityHasher` is the libstdc++-faithful default, `BuildMixingHasher` is the correct choice for unknown key distributions, and the overflow list guarantees correctness (never a hang, never a lost key) at the cost of throughput.

Overflow-list correctness hazards. `Pos` values above `slots()` index a `Vec` that `remove()` can shift and that `rehash` empties — so a `Pos` obtained before any mutation is dangling in the logical sense (wrong element, not memory-unsafe). Document `Pos` invalidation exactly as C++ documents iterator invalidation, and make `entry_at` return `Option` rather than panicking. Related: `pos_after` must handle the bucket->overflow transition (return `Pos(slots())` when the bucket scan runs out AND overflow is non-empty), or the last bucket entry's successor silently becomes `end` and `equal_range` on an overflow-resident key returns an empty range — a 1-that-prints-0 bug that only shows up under a clustering hasher.

Bit-shift and index arithmetic in `place` are the most bug-prone lines in the design. `1u32 << (free - home)` panics in debug and is UB-ish in release if `free - home >= 32`, so the hop-back while-loop must run to completion BEFORE the shift; the candidate window `free + 1 - NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE` underflows if computed while `free < NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE - 1`, so it must be guarded by the same `free - home >= NEIGHBOURHOOD_SIZE` condition; and the bitmap update on a move must clear the OLD bit before setting the new one, using the entry's own home `ch`, not the inserting key's `home`. A single dropped `&= !(1 << ..)` produces a bitmap claiming an occupancy that is not there, which makes `find` return a wrong-key slot. Mitigation: a `#[cfg(test)] fn assert_invariants()` that walks every bucket, recomputes each entry's home, and asserts the bitmap matches exactly — called after every insert in a randomized test with a deliberately terrible `ConstantHasher`.

`i * 12` will PANIC in the standalone build for large counts. VERIFIED that plain `rustc` with no `-O` enables overflow checks (rustc even rejected a constant-folded `200000000i32 * 12` at compile time as a hard error). C++ wraps; a Rust debug build aborts with exit 101 and a totally different message. Use `i.wrapping_mul(12)`. The same class of bug lurks in any `as usize` on `count`, and in `bucket_count * 2` / `next_power_of_two()` near `usize::MAX` (guard the growth arithmetic even though allocation fails first in practice).

Three distinct death modes are easy to collapse into two or one. Missing `argv[2]` is a `std::logic_error` with `what() == "basic_string::_S_construct null not valid"` (no `stoi` anywhere in it), `no digits` is `std::invalid_argument`/`stoi`, and `out of int range` is `std::out_of_range`/`stoi`. In Rust `args_os().nth(2)` is just `None`, so the tempting `unwrap_or(15)` / `if let Ok(n)` shapes silently convert two required aborts into a success printing 1. Keeping `StoiError` and `Fault` as separate two- and two-variant enums, with the message strings living only in `terminate.rs`, is what prevents this.

The stderr text is byte-exact and unreviewable by eye: two-space indent before `what():`, then TWO spaces before the message. I confirmed a hand-written Rust message `cmp`s identical to the C++ binary's 87 bytes, but the way to keep it that way is a `#[test]` asserting the exact literal from the pure `message()` helper (the abort itself cannot be unit-tested in-process without killing the harness). Also: `std::process::abort()`, never `process::exit(134)` — the number in `$?` matches but `WIFSIGNALED` and the core dump do not.

`std::env::args()` panics on non-UTF-8 argv while the C++ binary returns 5 for bytes `0x35 0xFF`. The whole `Argv` type exists to force `args_os()` + `OsStrExt::as_bytes()`; on a non-unix target `as_bytes` does not exist (`as_encoded_bytes`, stabilized 1.74, is the portable spelling). Toolchain here is rustc 1.75.0, so either works, but `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt` pins the file to unix — acceptable given the reference binary is a Linux ELF, worth a comment.

Over-abstraction is a genuine risk for a program whose entire output is one of two characters. Four `tsl` files plus three `cxx` files plus `app.rs` is a lot of surface for `println!("{}", 0_or_1)`, and every public method that the bin does not call is dead code the compiler will warn about under BOTH build paths (hence the `#![allow(dead_code, unused_imports)]` at each layer facade — which in turn hides genuine dead-code signals). Mitigation: justify each layer by what it makes testable (the `hash` split is what let me price three hashers; the `Pos` split is what keeps the hop-back loop lifetime-free; the `cxx::stoi` split is what turns ~90 spec vectors into ordinary unit tests) and resist adding API beyond the C++ surface plus the idiomatic-Rust companions listed above.

Silent divergence between `equal_range` and `count` is the failure this port exists to catch, and it will not show up at count=15. The distance-1 property depends on `insert` refusing to overwrite duplicates, on the bitmap invariant surviving rehash, and on `pos_after` being correct at both boundaries (the found element being LAST in iteration order, so `range.second == end`, is the count=2 case). Test at the resize boundaries the spec singled out — 1, 2, 4095/4096/4097, 65535/65536/65537 — and assert `equal_range(&k).count() == map.count(&k)` for every key, plus `map.len() == count`, which is what catches a resize that loses or duplicates entries.
